# Commits whose MESSAGES match a leak pattern and are accepted anyway.
#
# Same posture as leak-allowlist.txt and leak-allow-strings.txt: deny by
# default, and every exception is one explicit reviewable line rather than a
# widened pattern.
#
# Why by COMMIT and not by string. Allowlisting the matched text would permit
# it in every future commit message too, which retires the rule instead of
# making an exception to it. A commit message is immutable history; the only
# way to change one is to rewrite the branch. So the exception belongs to the
# commit, and a NEW commit containing the same text still fails.
#
# This also means a rewritten commit loses its exception, because its SHA
# changes. That is deliberate — a rewritten message is a new message and
# deserves a fresh judgement. It is also why the branch carrying an excepted
# commit must be MERGED forward, never rebased.
#
# ⚠️ A SQUASH MERGE IS A REWRITE. GitHub's squash button folds every branch
# message into one new commit, so an excepted message reappears under a new SHA
# and the scan fails on the merge — after the merge, when main is already red.
# This is not hypothetical; it happened on the first PR this file protected.
# When you merge a branch carrying an entry below, expect to add the resulting
# commit here too, or use a merge commit instead of a squash so the original
# SHAs survive.
#
# Full 40-character SHAs, one per line, each with a comment saying what the
# message contains and who decided to accept it.

# Contains a reference to an internal planning document, by number and section.
# Described rather than quoted: reproducing the matched text here would put the
# disclosure into a tracked file, which is worse than leaving it in one immutable
# commit message. Same reasoning as the header of leak-patterns.txt.
# Reviewed 2026-09-03 and accepted deliberately: the message is an engineer's
# post-mortem of a token-lifetime mistake (a 4m58s credential against a 8m56s
# build) and carries no credential, hostname, or infrastructure detail. The
# commit was already public when this was found, so rewriting it would not have
# unpublished it. The reference itself is the whole of the disclosure.
9a8275cd73f0f6b7a0e26f20b8fceb3e593444c4

# The squash merge of the pull request that carried the commit above. GitHub
# folded that message into this new commit, so the same reference reappeared
# under a new SHA and the scan failed on main immediately after the merge.
# Same content, same decision as above — not a second judgement, the same one
# applied to the commit that now carries the text.
947c9ceaca2cf20661e489a4abe17f3a8d1f596a

# Contains one internal migration identifier, in a paragraph explaining why a
# destroy-then-recreate cycle needed a schema change. Described rather than
# quoted, per the header above.
# Reviewed 2026-09-03 and accepted: the string names a private repo's migration
# numbering and nothing else — no credential, hostname, account id, or
# infrastructure detail. It was already public when found, and main carries
# three signed release tags, so rewriting history would break every clone and
# every published checksum to unpublish a string that is already indexed.
# The pattern that catches this class was added in the same change, so the tree
# is clean and the NEXT one fails rather than being accepted.
4d3220b5a471d02f18cad3f5642a5c653df9e63e
